title: Functional dependencies and normal forms
subtitle: Bad table design makes data contradict itself. Functional dependencies say exactly which designs are bad.

sections.title: Why design matters: update anomalies
sections.body: Suppose one table holds (student, course, instructor, instructor office). The office is repeated on every enrolment. Change an instructor’s office and you must update many rows — forget one and the data disagrees (update anomaly). A new instructor with no students cannot be recorded (insertion anomaly); deleting the last enrolment loses the instructor’s details (deletion anomaly). Normalisation removes them by splitting tables.

questions.prompt: Repeating an instructor’s office on every enrolment row risks…

choices.text: An update anomaly: changing it in some rows but not others.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The fact is stored many times.

sections.title: Functional dependencies and closure
sections.body: X → Y (a functional dependency) means any two rows that agree on X agree on Y — e.g. studentID → name. The closure X⁺ is everything X determines: start with X and keep adding the right side of any dependency whose left side is already present. For R(A,B,C,D,E) with A→B, B→C, CD→E: A⁺ = ABC... it stops at ABC because E needs D as well.

worked.why: Is AD a key of R(A,B,C,D,E)? Compute (AD)⁺.
AD → B (A→B) → C (B→C) → E (CD→E). Every attribute is reached.
Neither A nor D alone reaches everything, so AD is a candidate key (minimal).

choices.text: All attributes functionally determined by X.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: If X⁺ is every attribute, X is a superkey.

figures.note: Closure steps, then keys, then the normal-form check.

sections.title: Finding candidate keys
sections.body: Attributes that appear on no right-hand side must be in every key. Compute their closure; if it covers everything, you are done, otherwise add more attributes. For the example the key is AD. Prime attributes are those in some candidate key.

questions.prompt: An attribute that never appears on the right of any FD…

choices.text: Must belong to every candidate key.

problems.prompt: R(A,B,C,D,E) with A→B, B→C, CD→E. Find the candidate key(s).
problems.answer: Attributes A and D are never on a right-hand side, so both are in every key; (AD)⁺ = ABCDE, so the only candidate key is AD.

sections.title: 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF
sections.body: 1NF: every cell holds one atomic value. 2NF: 1NF and no partial dependency — no non-prime attribute depends on part of a candidate key. 3NF: 2NF and no transitive dependency — for every X→A, X is a superkey or A is prime. BCNF: for every X→A, X is a superkey (stricter). Examples from the checker: R(A,B,C) with A→B, B→C is 2NF (B→C is transitive); R(A,B,C,D) with AB→C, B→D is 1NF (D depends on part of the key AB); R(A,B,C) with AB→C, C→B is 3NF (C→B is allowed in 3NF since B is prime, but C is not a superkey).

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Every determinant must be a superkey.

sections.title: Decomposition
sections.body: To remove a violation, split the table along the offending dependency: for A→B→C, split R(A,B,C) into R1(A,B) and R2(B,C). A good decomposition is lossless (joining the parts gives back exactly the original — the common attributes must be a key of one part) and ideally dependency-preserving. Denormalising (re-joining) is sometimes chosen deliberately for read speed.

worked.why: Decompose R(A,B,C) with A→B, B→C to 3NF.
R1(A,B) and R2(B,C). Common attribute B is a key of R2, so the join is lossless.

questions.prompt: A decomposition into R1 and R2 is lossless when…

choices.text: Their common attributes are a key of R1 or R2.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: Then the join would be a product.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Then the natural join returns exactly the original rows.

sections.title: Integrity constraints and assertions
sections.body: Domain constraints restrict values (age > 0); key and NOT NULL constraints; referential integrity (foreign keys); CHECK conditions and general assertions; triggers for richer rules. The DBMS refuses updates that violate them.

questions.prompt: Referential integrity requires a foreign-key value to…

choices.text: Match an existing key in the referenced table (or be NULL).

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: You cannot enrol in a course that does not exist.
